outcomes.text: Explain that all living things share a similar biochemical basis.
Define monomers and polymers, with monosaccharides, amino acids and nucleotides as examples.
Describe condensation reactions that join molecules and release water.
Describe hydrolysis reactions that break bonds using water.
Name common monosaccharides: glucose, galactose, fructose.
Explain how a condensation reaction forms a glycosidic bond.
Say how maltose, sucrose and lactose form from monosaccharides.
Distinguish alpha-glucose from beta-glucose.
Describe how polysaccharides form from many glucose units; glycogen and starch from alpha-glucose, cellulose from beta-glucose.
Relate the structure and function of glycogen, starch and cellulose in animal and plant cells.
Do Benedict's tests for reducing and non-reducing sugars and the iodine test for starch.
Describe how a triglyceride forms from glycerol and three fatty acids through ester bonds.
Tell saturated from unsaturated fatty acids from diagrams.
Describe how phospholipids differ from triglycerides in structure and explain their different properties.
Carry out the emulsion test for lipids.
Describe the general structure of an amino acid and say that the 20 common amino acids differ in side group.
Explain how condensation forms peptide bonds, dipeptides and polypeptides.
Say that a functional protein may contain one or more polypeptides.
Explain the roles of hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds and disulfide bridges in protein structure.
Relate primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure to protein function.
Carry out the biuret test for proteins.
Explain how enzymes lower activation energy.
Describe the induced-fit model of enzyme action.
Relate an enzyme's properties to the tertiary structure of its active site and enzyme-substrate complex formation.
Explain enzyme specificity.
Appreciate how models of enzyme action have changed and that enzymes catalyse many intracellular and extracellular reactions.
Explain the effects of enzyme and substrate concentration, competitive and non-competitive inhibitors, pH and temperature on reaction rate.
Required practical 1: investigate how a named variable affects the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction.

topics.title: 3.1.5 Nucleic acids are important information-carrying molecules

outcomes.text: Describe the roles of DNA and RNA in carrying genetic information and ribosome composition.
Describe nucleotide components of DNA and RNA and the phosphodiester bond.
Describe DNA as a double helix with hydrogen bonded complementary base pairs, and RNA as a short single chain.
Appreciate why DNA's simplicity made scientists doubt it carried the genetic code.
Explain why semi-conservative replication ensures genetic continuity.
Describe replication: unwinding, breaking hydrogen bonds with helicase, base pairing to templates, and DNA polymerase joining nucleotides.
Evaluate the work validating the Watson-Crick model of replication.
Describe the structure of ATP.
Explain hydrolysis of ATP to ADP and Pi by ATP hydrolase and its coupling to energy-requiring reactions.
Explain how released phosphate can phosphorylate and activate other compounds.
Explain ATP resynthesis by ATP synthase in photosynthesis or respiration.
Explain that water is a metabolite in condensation and hydrolysis reactions and a solvent for metabolic reactions.
Explain how water's high heat capacity buffers temperature change.
Explain how water's high latent heat of vaporisation gives cooling with little water loss.
Explain how cohesion supports water columns in plants and creates surface tension.
Explain that each ion has a specific role depending on its properties.
Recognise ion roles: hydrogen ions and pH, iron in haemoglobin, sodium in co-transport, phosphate in DNA and ATP.
Describe the structure and function of the cell-surface membrane, nucleus, mitochondria and chloroplasts.
Describe the structure and function of the Golgi apparatus, lysosomes, ribosomes, rough and smooth ER, cell wall and vacuole.
Explain how specialised cells are organised into tissues, organs and systems, and explain cell adaptations.
Compare prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells: size, organelles, ribosomes, DNA and murein cell wall.
Name optional prokaryote features: plasmids, capsule, flagella.
Describe viruses as acellular and non-living, with genetic material, capsid and attachment protein.
Explain the principles and limits of optical, transmission and scanning electron microscopes.
Measure object size under an optical microscope and distinguish magnification from resolution.
Use magnification = image size / real size.
Describe cell fractionation and ultracentrifugation, and how artefacts were told from organelles.

topics.title: 3.2.2 All cells arise from other cells

outcomes.text: Explain that only some cells in multicellular organisms keep dividing, with a cell cycle.
Describe DNA replication in interphase and mitosis producing identical daughter cells.
Describe chromosome behaviour in each mitosis stage and the role of spindle fibres, and cytokinesis.
Recognise cell cycle stages and explain cell appearance in each stage of mitosis.
Explain how uncontrolled division forms tumours and how treatments target division rate.
Describe binary fission in prokaryotes including replication of DNA and plasmids.
Explain that viruses do not divide but are replicated by infected host cells.
Required practical 2: stain root tip squashes, identify mitosis stages, calculate a mitotic index and actual cell size.
Explain that all cell membranes share the same basic structure.
Describe the fluid-mosaic model: phospholipids, proteins, glycoproteins, glycolipids, and cholesterol's role.
Explain simple diffusion and its limits imposed by the phospholipid bilayer.
Explain facilitated diffusion with carrier and channel proteins.
Explain osmosis in terms of water potential.
Explain active transport with carrier proteins and ATP hydrolysis.
Explain co-transport using sodium ion and glucose absorption in the ileum.
Explain how cells are adapted for rapid transport with larger area or more channels and carriers.
Explain how surface area, protein numbers and gradients affect transport rate.
Required practical 3: make a dilution series and calibration curve to find plant tissue water potential.
Required practical 4: investigate a variable's effect on cell-surface membrane permeability.

topics.title: 3.2.4 Cell recognition and the immune system

outcomes.text: Explain how surface molecules let the immune system identify pathogens, other-species cells, abnormal cells and toxins.
Define antigen and explain effects of antigen variability.
Describe phagocytosis and destruction of pathogens by lysozymes.
Describe the T lymphocyte response, including antigen-presenting cells.
Describe helper T cells stimulating cytotoxic T cells, B cells and phagocytes.
Describe B lymphocyte response, clonal selection and monoclonal antibody release.
Define antibody, describe its structure, and explain antigen-antibody complexes and agglutination.
Explain plasma and memory cells in primary and secondary responses.
Explain how vaccines protect individuals and populations, with herd immunity.
Distinguish active from passive immunity.
Describe HIV structure and replication in helper T cells.
Explain how HIV causes AIDS symptoms and why antibiotics don't work on viruses.
Describe monoclonal antibodies in targeted drug delivery and diagnosis, and the ELISA test.
Discuss ethical issues and evaluate evidence on vaccines and monoclonal antibodies.

units.title: 3.3 Organisms exchange substances with their environment

outcomes.text: Relate organism size to surface area to volume ratio.
Explain body shape changes and systems in larger organisms as adaptations to a falling ratio.
Appreciate the link between surface area to volume ratio and metabolic rate.
Describe gas exchange in single-celled organisms, insect tracheal systems, fish gills with counter-current flow, and dicot leaves.
Explain compromises between gas exchange and water loss in insects and xerophytes.

subtopics.title: Human gas exchange and lung disease

outcomes.text: Describe the human gas exchange system and alveolar epithelium features.
Explain ventilation, with the diaphragm and intercostal muscles changing thoracic pressure.
Interpret data on lung disease, smoking and pollution, risk factors and restrictions; tell correlation from causation.
Explain hydrolysis of large molecules during digestion.
Describe digestion of carbohydrates by amylases and disaccharidases, lipids by lipase and bile salts, proteins by peptidases.
Explain absorption in the ileum: co-transport of amino acids and monosaccharides, and micelles for lipids.
Describe haemoglobin's quaternary structure and role in oxygen transport.
Explain loading and unloading of oxygen with the dissociation curve and cooperative binding.
Explain the Bohr effect and animal haemoglobin variations.
Describe mammalian blood circulation and main vessels named.
Describe the heart's structure and the pressure, volume and valve changes of the cardiac cycle.
Analyse cardiac cycle data.
Relate structure of arteries, arterioles and veins to function.
Describe capillary structure, capillary beds and tissue fluid formation and return.
Analyse data on cardiovascular risk factors, evaluate conflicting evidence, and recognise correlation and causation.
Required practical 5: dissect an animal or plant gas exchange or transport system.
Describe xylem water transport and the cohesion-tension theory.
Describe phloem transport of organic substances and the mass flow hypothesis.
Interpret tracer and ringing experiments and evaluate evidence for and against mass flow, noting correlations and causation.

units.title: 3.4 Genetic information, variation and relationships between organisms

outcomes.text: Compare DNA in prokaryotes (short, circular, no proteins) with eukaryotic nuclear DNA (long, linear, with histones) and organelle DNA.
Define a gene as a base sequence coding for a polypeptide or functional RNA, at a fixed locus.
Explain that a triplet codes an amino acid and that the code is universal, non-overlapping and degenerate.
Describe non-coding DNA, repeats, exons and introns in eukaryotes.
Define genome and proteome.
Describe the structure of mRNA and tRNA.
Describe transcription and RNA polymerase, in prokaryotes and in eukaryotes with pre-mRNA splicing.
Describe translation with ribosomes, tRNA and ATP.
Relate nucleic acid base sequence to amino acid sequence from supplied code data and interpret experimental data.

topics.title: 3.4.3 Genetic diversity can arise as a result of mutation or during meiosis

outcomes.text: Describe gene mutations (deletion, substitution), how they arise and why some substitutions have no effect.
Explain mutagenic agents and chromosome non-disjunction in meiosis.
Describe meiosis: two nuclear divisions producing four haploid cells from a diploid cell.
Explain variation from independent segregation and crossing over.
Complete diagrams of chromosome content after each division and explain the different outcomes of mitosis and meiosis.
Recognise where meiosis occurs in an unfamiliar life cycle.
Explain how random fertilisation adds genetic variation.
Define genetic diversity as the number of alleles in a population and explain why it enables natural selection.
Explain natural selection: mutation, advantage, inheritance and rising allele frequency.
Explain directional selection (antibiotic resistance) and stabilising selection (birth weight).
Describe anatomical, physiological and behavioural adaptations.
Use unfamiliar information and data to explain how selection changes a population.
Show understanding that adaptation and selection drive evolution and diversity.
Required practical 6: use aseptic technique to test antimicrobial substances on microbial growth.
Define a species by fertile offspring and explain courtship's role in recognition.
Describe phylogenetic hierarchy: domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.
Explain binomial naming, and how immunology and genome sequencing clarify evolutionary relationships.
Explain biodiversity across habitat scales and define species richness.
Explain an index of diversity and calculate it with d = N(N-1) / sum n(n-1).
Explain how farming reduces biodiversity and the conservation balance.
Compare diversity via characteristics, DNA, mRNA or protein amino acid sequences.
Interpret sequence data to suggest relationships within and between species.
Appreciate that direct DNA investigation replaced inference from characteristics.
Collect data from random samples, calculate means and standard deviations, and interpret them.

units.title: 3.5 Energy transfers in and between organisms (A-level only)

outcomes.text: Describe chlorophyll photoionisation, ATP and reduced NADP production.
Explain electron transfer chain, proton movement and ATP synthase (chemiosmotic theory).
Explain photolysis of water giving protons, electrons and oxygen.
Describe CO2 reacting with RuBP, catalysed by rubisco, to form GP.
Explain GP reduction to triose phosphate using ATP and reduced NADP.
Explain RuBP regeneration in the Calvin cycle and triose phosphate conversion into useful substances.
Identify factors that limit photosynthesis and evaluate agricultural practices that overcome them.
Required practical 7: chromatography of leaf pigments.
Required practical 8: factor effects on dehydrogenase activity in chloroplast extracts.
Describe glycolysis in the cytoplasm: phosphorylation, triose phosphate, oxidation to pyruvate with net ATP and reduced NAD.
Explain conversion of pyruvate to ethanol or lactate to regenerate NAD in anaerobic respiration.
Describe active transport of pyruvate into the mitochondrial matrix and its oxidation to acetate.
Describe the link reaction producing acetylcoenzyme A.
Describe the Krebs cycle: reduced coenzymes, substrate-level phosphorylation and CO2 loss.
Describe oxidative phosphorylation with the electron transfer chain and chemiosmosis.
Explain how lipid and amino acid breakdown products enter the Krebs cycle.
Required practical 9: investigate a variable's effect on respiration rate of single-celled organisms.
Explain how plants use sugars for respiration and biomass, and measure biomass by carbon or dry mass and calorimetry.
Define GPP and NPP (NPP = GPP - R).
Calculate consumer net production N = I - (F + R).
Define primary and secondary productivity as a rate, e.g. kJ per ha per year.
Appreciate how farming raises energy transfer efficiency by simplifying food webs and reducing respiratory losses.
Describe nutrient recycling, e.g. nitrogen and phosphorus cycles, and the role of saprobionts and mycorrhizae.
Describe bacterial roles in the nitrogen cycle: ammonification, nitrification, nitrogen fixation, denitrification.
Explain use of natural and artificial fertilisers, and leaching and eutrophication.

units.title: 3.6 Organisms respond to changes in their internal and external environments (A-level only)

topics.title: 3.6.1 Stimuli, both internal and external, are detected and lead to a response

outcomes.text: Explain how responding to the environment increases survival.
Explain plant growth factors, and IAA's effect on cell elongation in roots and shoots explaining gravitropism and phototropism.
Describe taxes and kineses as simple responses keeping organisms in favourable environments.
Explain the protective role of a three-neurone simple reflex.
Required practical 10: investigate an environmental variable's effect on animal movement using a choice chamber or maze.
Use the Pacinian corpuscle to show receptors respond only to specific stimuli and produce a generator potential.
Describe its structure and how stretch-mediated sodium channels deform to give a generator potential.
Explain how rods, cones and optic nerve connections give differences in light sensitivity, colour sensitivity and visual acuity.
Describe myogenic stimulation and the roles of SAN, AVN and Purkyne tissue in the bundle of His.
Describe chemoreceptors, pressure receptors and the autonomic nervous system controlling heart rate.
Describe the structure of a myelinated motor neurone.
Explain the resting potential from differential permeability and sodium and potassium movement.
Explain depolarisation, the action potential and the all-or-nothing principle.
Describe action potentials along non-myelinated and myelinated axons.
Explain the refractory period's role in discrete impulses and frequency limits.
Explain how myelination, saltatory conduction, axon diameter and temperature affect conduction speed.
Describe the detailed structure of a synapse and neuromuscular junction.
Explain cholinergic synapse transmission, unidirectionality, summation and inhibition.
Compare transmission at a cholinergic synapse and a neuromuscular junction.
Predict and explain the effects of drugs on a synapse from given information.

topics.title: 3.6.3 Skeletal muscles are stimulated to contract by nerves and act as effectors

outcomes.text: Explain antagonistic muscle pairs against an incompressible skeleton.
Describe gross and microscopic skeletal muscle structure and myofibril ultrastructure.
Explain roles of actin, myosin, calcium ions and ATP in contraction.
Explain calcium ions and tropomyosin in actinomyosin bridge formation.
Explain roles of ATP and phosphocreatine in contraction.
Describe slow and fast skeletal muscle fibres.

topics.title: 3.6.4 Homeostasis is the maintenance of a stable internal environment

outcomes.text: Explain how homeostasis keeps the internal environment within limits.
Explain why stable core temperature, blood pH and blood glucose matter.
Explain negative feedback and why separate mechanisms for each direction give better control.
Interpret information on negative and positive feedback examples.
Explain factors influencing blood glucose and the liver's roles in glycogenesis, glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.
Explain the actions of insulin, glucagon and adrenaline on target cells.
Explain the second messenger model with adenylate cyclase, cAMP and protein kinase.
Explain causes of type I and II diabetes and their control.
Evaluate positions of health advisers and the food industry on type II diabetes.
Required practical 11: dilution series and colorimetry to find glucose in a 'urine' sample.
Explain osmoregulation and the roles of hypothalamus, posterior pituitary and ADH.
Describe nephron structure and roles in glomerular filtrate formation, proximal tubule reabsorption, loop of Henle sodium gradient and distal tubule and collecting duct water reabsorption.

units.title: 3.7 Genetics, populations, evolution and ecosystems (A-level only)

outcomes.text: Define genotype and phenotype.
Explain multiple alleles, dominant, recessive and codominant alleles, and homozygous and heterozygous.
Use labelled genetic diagrams for monohybrid and dihybrid crosses with dominant, recessive and codominant alleles.
Use genetic diagrams for sex-linkage, autosomal linkage, multiple alleles and epistasis.
Use the chi-squared test to compare observed and expected phenotypic ratios.
Define a population, gene pool and allele frequency.
Explain the Hardy-Weinberg principle and its conditions.
Calculate allele, genotype and phenotype frequencies with p2 + 2pq + q2 = 1.

topics.title: 3.7.3 Evolution may lead to speciation (A-level only)

outcomes.text: Explain phenotype variation from genetic and environmental factors, with mutation as primary source and meiosis and fertilisation adding more.
Explain natural selection by predation, disease and competition and its effect on allele frequencies.
Describe stabilising, directional and disruptive selection.
Define evolution as change in allele frequency.
Explain genetic drift and why it matters in small populations.
Explain how reproductive separation causes new species, including allopatric and sympatric speciation.
Explain how selection and isolation change frequencies and form species, and how long-term change produced diversity.
Define community and ecosystem and explain niche.
Explain carrying capacity and effects of abiotic factors, competition and predation on population size.
Estimate population size with quadrats, belt transects and mark-release-recapture and state its assumptions.
Describe primary succession from pioneer species to climax community.
Explain how organisms change their abiotic environment and biodiversity.
Explain conservation management of succession and the conflict between human needs and conservation.
Evaluate conservation evidence and calculate population size from mark-release-recapture data.
Required practical 12: investigate an environmental factor's effect on a species' distribution.

units.title: 3.8 The control of gene expression (A-level only)

topics.title: 3.8.1 Alteration of the sequence of bases in DNA can alter the structure of proteins

outcomes.text: Describe gene mutation types: addition, deletion, substitution, inversion, duplication, translocation.
Explain that mutations occur spontaneously and mutagenic agents raise the rate.
Explain single-triplet changes and why degeneracy means not all change the amino acid.
Explain frame shifts and relate a mutation's nature to its effect on the polypeptide.

topics.title: 3.8.2 Gene expression is controlled by a number of features

outcomes.text: Explain that totipotent cells make any cell type, translate only part of their DNA, and occur briefly in early embryos.
Distinguish pluripotent, multipotent and unipotent cells, with cardiomyocytes as an example.
Explain induced pluripotent stem cells made from somatic cells with transcription factors.
Evaluate stem cell use in treating disorders.
Explain how transcription factors entering the nucleus stimulate or inhibit transcription, with oestrogen as an example.
Explain epigenetics: heritable changes without base changes, through DNA methylation or reduced histone acetylation.
Explain epigenetics in disease and cancer.
Explain RNA interference inhibiting translation.
Interpret gene expression data and evaluate genetic versus environmental influences on phenotype.
Describe benign and malignant tumour characteristics.
Explain roles of tumour suppressor genes, oncogenes, abnormal methylation and raised oestrogen in tumour development.
Evaluate correlations between genetic and environmental factors and cancer.
Interpret how knowledge of oncogenes and suppressor genes helps prevention, treatment and cure.
Explain genome sequencing projects across organisms including humans.
Explain how simple organisms' genomes give their proteomes, e.g. to find vaccine antigens.
Explain why non-coding DNA and regulatory genes stop genome knowledge translating easily to proteome in complex organisms.
Appreciate that sequencing methods are updated and automated.
Describe recombinant DNA technology and why transferred DNA works in a transgenic organism.
Describe producing fragments by cDNA via reverse transcriptase, restriction enzymes, or a gene machine.
Explain PCR as an in vitro method of amplification.
Explain culturing transformed host cells as in vivo amplification.
Describe adding promoter and terminator regions and using restriction endonucleases, ligases and vectors for transformation.
Explain marker genes for detecting GM cells.
Interpret information on recombinant DNA technology.
Evaluate ethical, financial and social issues of its use and ownership in agriculture, industry and medicine.
Balance humanitarian aspects against environmentalist and anti-globalisation opposition, and relate it to gene therapy.
Explain labelled DNA probes and hybridisation to find specific alleles.
Explain screening for heritable conditions, drug responses and health risks, and use in genetic counselling and personalised medicine.
Evaluate information on screening for genetically determined conditions and drug responses.
Explain VNTRs and why two people rarely share the same ones.
Describe genetic fingerprinting of PCR-cloned fragments for relationships and population variability.
Explain uses in forensics, medical diagnosis and animal and plant breeding.
Interpret gel electrophoresis results for DNA fragments.
